claim: The Warehouse's period of significance was 1977-1982, and its address was 206 S. Jefferson Street, Chicago; the City of Chicago designated the building a landmark (2023).
source: City of Chicago, Landmark Designation Report for The Warehouse (2023)
evidence: Landmark report cover and text identify 206 S. Jefferson and the 1977-1982 period of significance; designation approved June 2023 (chicago.gov DCA announcement).
notes: Do not conflate the city-designated period of significance with a settled founding-year narrative; founding year itself is treated as DISPUTED (see CL-41).

claim: The Warehouse relocated from 555 W. Adams to 206 S. Jefferson Street in 1977.
source: City of Chicago DCA announcement (2024, chicago.gov); CTL-DR-MUSIC-001 timeline
evidence: City announcement states the 1977 relocation; CTL-DR-MUSIC-001 independently graded this Verified.
notes: The relocation is city-attested; exact move mechanics not detailed.

claim: Promoter Robert Williams founded the Warehouse, ran 'US Studios' loft parties, first offered the DJ residency to Larry Levan (1976), who declined and recommended Frankie Knuckles.
source: City of Chicago, Landmark Designation Report for The Warehouse (2023)
evidence: Report documents Williams seeking Levan and Knuckles in 1976, Levan's refusal (Paradise Garage), and the recommendation of Knuckles.
notes: A CTL-DR-MUSIC-001 entity gives '(228 S. Jefferson)' for the Warehouse; the report's map shows 228 S. Jefferson as a separate building label, not the Warehouse. That entity is in error; the Warehouse is 206 S. Jefferson.

claim: Frankie Knuckles arrived in Chicago in March 1977 and became the Warehouse's resident DJ.
source: City of Chicago, Landmark Designation Report for The Warehouse (2023)
evidence: 'Knuckles arrived in March 1977, moving into an ad hoc living quarter in 206 S. Jefferson.'

claim: The Warehouse's crowd was Black, Latino, and largely gay.
source: City of Chicago, Landmark Designation Report for The Warehouse (2023); Red Bull Music Academy Daily (2015-05)
evidence: Report describes the Black/Latino, largely gay congregation; cited by CTL-DR-MUSIC-001 red team as Verified.
notes: The queer-of-color social form is structural to the scene, per oral histories.

claim: Frankie Knuckles was an out gay man whose work is rooted in Black gay club culture.
source: Chicago LGBT Hall of Fame (chicagolgbthalloffame.org/knuckles-frankie/)
evidence: Hall of Fame entry documents Knuckles as an out gay DJ/producer/remixer and ties the Warehouse and house music to Black gay community roots.

claim: Knuckles and Larry Levan learned their DJ craft together at the Continental Baths in New York, experimenting with mixing and re-presenting records as 'an art form.'
source: City of Chicago, Landmark Designation Report for The Warehouse (2023)
evidence: Report quotes Knuckles: 'Larry Levan and I would spend entire afternoons working up ideas on how to mix songs...'

claim: In 1983 Knuckles parted ways with Williams and opened the Power Plant at 1015 N. Halsted St.; Williams rebranded the Warehouse as the Music Box at a new location and hired Ron Hardy as resident.
source: City of Chicago, Landmark Designation Report for The Warehouse (2023)
evidence: Report text: Power Plant at 1015 N. Halsted on Goose Island; Warehouse rebranded as Music Box 'at a new location on Lower Wacker Drive' with Ron Hardy resident.
contradictory_evidence: Oral histories place the Music Box at 1632 S. Indiana Ave.; secondary references cite other addresses. The report's 'Lower Wacker' is one account among several.
notes: The rebrand + Hardy residency is Verified; the Music Box ADDRESS is DISPUTED (see CL-09).

claim: The Music Box opened in February 1983 with Ron Hardy as resident DJ.
source: CTL-DR-MUSIC-001 timeline (iHeart podcast; oral histories)
evidence: Oral histories date the opening to February 1983 and place it at 1632 S. Indiana Ave.; secondary references cite different addresses.
contradictory_evidence: Multiple competing address accounts (1632 S. Indiana vs. 326 N. [per secondary refs] vs. Lower Wacker per city report).
notes: Do not state the Music Box address as fact. CTL-DR-BMI-002 quarantined this contradiction.

claim: The Hot Mix 5 were assembled in 1981 by WBMX program director Lee Michaels for the 'Saturday Night Live, Ain't No Jive' show and broadcast live DJ mixes to a mass audience (city report: a million listeners per week).
source: City of Chicago, Landmark Designation Report (2023); Wikipedia 'Hot Mix 5' (with cited references)
evidence: Landmark report documents the WBMX Hot Mix 5 lineup's weekly reach; membership list (Farley 'Funkin' Keith, Mickey 'Mixin' Oliver, Ralphi Rosario, Kenny 'Jammin' Jason, Scott 'Smokin' Silz) per cited-reference sources.
notes: CTL-DR-MUSIC-001 graded the team/ratings claim Verified; exact ratings figures (2M listeners) rest on single sources.

claim: Jesse Saunders and Vince Lawrence co-created and pressed 'On & On' on the Jes Say label in January 1984, having tested it on cassette in clubs first.
source: WCSU/NPR 'From the Warehouse to the World' (2023-03-02); Gridface Vince Lawrence interview
evidence: Saunders/Lawrence corroborate joint creation, cassette club-testing, and January 1984 pressing.
contradictory_evidence: Rival 'first' claims (see CL-13, CL-32); Saunders's brother Wayne Williams has publicly questioned aspects of Saunders's account.
notes: Participant testimony is primary but interested-party; corroboration by Lawrence strengthens it.

claim: 'On & On' is 'generally accepted as the first house track committed to vinyl.'
source: Resident Advisor (ra.co/news/10915); NPR/KMUC 'This Old Chicago House: EDM's Family Roots' (2012)
evidence: RA's careful formulation is echoed across music press; the claim is consensus-within-a-frame (committed to vinyl).
contradictory_evidence: Unqualified 'first house record' claims are DISPUTED (see CL-13, CL-32). 'On and On' itself was based partly on a Mach 'On & On' bootleg megamix.
notes: Standing rule: say 'first committed to vinyl (1984),' never 'first house record, full stop.'

claim: Jamie Principle's 'Your Love' circulated on cassette in Chicago clubs before its vinyl release (Persona, 1986); the 1987 Trax version credited to Frankie Knuckles is contested.
source: Insomniac; Resident Advisor; Wikipedia 'Your Love (Jamie Principle song)'
evidence: Multiple music-press accounts confirm cassette-first circulation; Principle alleged in 2014 that Trax 'literally just stole my stuff.'
contradictory_evidence: Demo date given as 1982 vs. 1984 in different sources; Knuckles-credited Trax version reflects label practice, not authorship.
notes: Illustrates first-created vs. first-circulated vs. first-pressed distinctions.

claim: Disco Demolition Night took place July 12, 1979 at Comiskey Park: a WLUP/Steve Dahl anti-disco promotion that ended in a riot, field destruction, and a forfeited White Sox game.
source: Britannica ('Disco Demolition Night')
evidence: Britannica documents the 98-cent tickets, ~50,000 fans, dynamited crate of disco records, riot police, forfeit, 39 arrests.
contradictory_evidence: Dahl and Veeck dispute interpretations of the night's meaning (racist backlash vs. harmless promotion).
notes: Event facts are settled; the claim that it 'killed disco' or 'caused house' is DISPUTED (see CL-17).

claim: Knuckles popularized the phrase 'house music is disco's revenge,' expressing continuity between disco and house.
source: DJ Lady D interview ('The Rundown: Chicago News'); KPR/NPR 'From the Warehouse to the World' (2023)
evidence: Lady D: 'Frankie Knuckles actually popularized that statement, that House music is disco's revenge.'
notes: Continuity frame; direct causation from Disco Demolition is not supported.

claim: Knuckles recalled first hearing the phrase 'house music' on signage in a South Side tavern/bar window around 1980-81 ('We play house music').
source: City of Chicago Landmark Designation Report (2023, quoting Knuckles); Channel 4 'Pump Up the Volume' documentary account via Energy Flash
source_type: primary (Knuckles interview, quoted in government record)
evidence: Report quotes Knuckles's account at length; consistent with his RBMA 2011 interview.
contradictory_evidence: DJ Leonard 'Remix' Rroy claims he posted such a sign himself — a documented minority account.
notes: The Warehouse derivation of the name has the strongest evidence; Rroy's claim is recorded, not adopted.

claim: 'Frankie Knuckles invented house music' as a lone-inventor claim.
source: CTL-DR-MUSIC-001 mythology audit; City of Chicago landmark report (contains the compression); Resident Advisor
evidence: Evidence shows collective creation: Knuckles, Ron Hardy, Robert Williams, Hot Mix 5, Saunders/Lawrence, Jamie Principle, Marshall Jefferson, Larry Heard, Phuture, and others. Knuckles's Warehouse sets played disco/imports/reworked soul-funk, not 'house records' (no such thing existed).
contradictory_evidence: Popular obituaries, the 'Godfather of House' honorific, and the city report's own 'Knuckles created house' shorthand.
notes: Standing CTL rule per CTL-DR-MUSIC-001: never compress to a lone-inventor story.

claim: Phuture (DJ Pierre, Spanky/Earl Smith Jr., Herb J, founded 1985) recorded 'Acid Tracks' to tape; Ron Hardy club-tested it at the Music Box (reportedly playing it four times in one night); it was pressed on Trax in 1987 and is credited with defining acid house.
source: MusicRadar 'Everything you need to know about: acid house'; Wikipedia 'Phuture' (cited)
evidence: DJ Pierre's own account (via MusicRadar) of giving the track to Hardy; 1987 Trax pressing widely documented.
contradictory_evidence: 'First acid house record' is DISPUTED: Sleezy D/Adonis/Marshall Jefferson's 'I've Lost Control' appeared on vinyl in 1986, a year earlier (MusicRadar).
notes: Also illustrates club-tested-before-pressed dynamics.

claim: The Roland TB-303 (designed by Tadao Kikumoto, released 1981, discontinued 1984) was a commercial failure sold cheap second-hand; Phuture manipulated its filter/envelope in real time to create the squelching 'acid' bassline on 'Acid Tracks.'
source: Wikipedia 'Roland TB-303' (cited to Sound on Sound, Guardian, Roland); MusicRadar; Wikipedia 'Acid house'
evidence: Design history and commercial failure documented via Sound on Sound/Guardian; Phuture's real-time manipulation documented via DJ Pierre's accounts.
contradictory_evidence: Production-run figures differ (10,000 vs. 20,000 in different sources); Charanjit Singh's 1982 'Synthesizing' is a documented earlier 303 use (Guardian, 2011) — a precursor, not acid house.
notes: The 'acid' name's LSD etymology is UNRESOLVED folk etymology; DJ Pierre (ADE 2023 panel) attributed it to the sound's quality.

claim: Farley 'Jackmaster' Funk's 'Love Can't Turn Around' (written by Vince Lawrence, sung by Darryl Pandy) reached the UK Top 10 in 1986.
source: WCSU/NPR 'From the Warehouse to the World' (2023); KPR/NPR
evidence: WCSU documents the release, writing, vocal, and UK chart run.
notes: Key evidence for the 1986 UK-diffusion chapter.

claim: Steve 'Silk' Hurley's 'Jack Your Body' reached #1 on the UK singles chart in 1987.
source: nightlife.fandom.com (Fandom wiki)
evidence: Single tertiary source; no primary or reputable-journalism confirmation located in this pass.
notes: Needs corroboration before publication; do not assert without sourcing.

claim: Marshall Jefferson's 'Move Your Body' (1986) established the piano-led anthem as a foundational house sound.
source: Grammy.com (Marshall Jefferson feature); Wikipedia 'Move Your Body (Marshall Jefferson song)'
evidence: Grammy.com documents the 1986 Trax release and its foundational role.
contradictory_evidence: CTL-DR-BMI-002 quarantines the 'first label: Trax vs. DJ International' question — unresolved.
notes: CTL-DR-MUSIC-001 graded this Verified; single-institutional-source basis keeps it at SUPPORTED here.

claim: DJ International Records was co-founded in 1985 by Rocky Jones and Benji Espinoza.
source: DJ Mag (Benji Espinoza obituary; Rocky Jones quoted account)
evidence: DJ Mag documents co-founding and Jones's record-pool origin account.
contradictory_evidence: Some histories credit Jones alone, erasing Espinoza.

claim: Trax Records' founding year (late 1984 vs. 1985) and founder credits (Larry Sherman; Vince Lawrence; others) are disputed; a 2022 lawsuit by Lawrence, Jefferson, Adonis, Maurice Joshua et al. alleged unpaid royalties, forged signatures, and bounced checks (allegations; outcome not established in sources reviewed).
source: DJ Mag (2022, Larry Sherman obituary + suit reporting); DJ Disc Jockey (2022); GO BANG Magazine (2020)
evidence: Multiple specialist-press reports of the 2022 suit; longstanding complaints of missing contracts/poor accounting.
confidence: medium (that the dispute exists); low (as to the allegations' merits)
contradictory_evidence: Label nostalgia framing Trax as a legitimate artist-friendly indie.
notes: Never present the allegations as adjudicated fact. Trax catalog rights are especially sensitive.

claim: The Chosen Few Disco Corp. was founded in 1977 by Wayne Williams with South Side DJs, part of the first wave that created house music.
source: Grooveist (2022); 5 Magazine (2015, 2019); Resident Advisor (2013, 2015)
evidence: Multiple independent music-press sources corroborate founding and picnic lineage (1990 Jackson Park picnic, 40,000+ attendees).
notes: Extends the story beyond the clubs to South Side mobile-DJ culture.

claim: Celeste Alexander (DJ Celeste), from Hyde Park, began DJing in 1982 and became one of Chicago's first female house DJs, later part of the all-female collective The Fantastic Four.
source: Chicago House Music Oral History Project, Center for Black Music Research (Micah Salkind interview); OkayAfrica
evidence: CBMR oral history details her training with Steve Hurley, Keith Fobbs, Andre Hatchett and first gig at Calvin Hollis' International Game Room.
notes: Single oral-history source; women remain structurally under-documented in house histories.

claim: Lori Branch entered the Warehouse scene in late 1979 and was spinning at teen-party battles and monthly parties by 1981, among Chicago's earliest female house DJs.
source: 'Everything House Music & More... The Podcast,' Ep. 50 (YouTube description)
evidence: Podcast episode description summarizing her oral-history interview.
notes: Sourced from a description, not the interview transcript; needs direct sourcing before publication.

claim: Imports Etc. was a Printers Row record store dealing exclusively in dance music ('the city's only...'), frequented by DJs; early Detroit techno innovators first encountered Chicago house there.
source: SPIN, 'Burning Down the House' (November 1986)
evidence: SPIN: 'the city's only record store dealing exclusively in dance music hangs its little yellow sign on a sealed-off garage door.'
notes: Retail as A&R/genre-formation infrastructure; the Detroit bridge claim rests on the same contemporary source.

claim: Gramaphone Records opened in 1969 and by the 1980s had shifted toward house and DJ vinyl, becoming a key record source for Chicago DJs.
source: Iowa Public Radio (2021)
evidence: Single public-media source.
notes: Needs corroboration.

claim: Larry Heard, recording as Mr. Fingers, produced deep-house landmarks ('Washing Machine,' 'Can You Feel It,' 'Beyond the Clouds') from a South Side base; his Fingers Inc. collaboration with Robert Owens brought soulful songwriting into early house.
source: NPR Illinois (2016-09-16); WCSU/NPR (2023)
evidence: NPR Illinois documents the South Side context and key tracks; WCSU documents Owens's role.
notes: CTL-DR-MUSIC-001 graded both claims Verified.

claim: Z-Factor's 'Fantasy' was recorded in 1983 and released in March 1984 on Mitchbal, and is a candidate for earliest house track pressed to vinyl.
source: Hyperreal 'Sample and Hold - The House Sound of Chicago' (music.hyperreal.org)
evidence: Hyperreal history argues 'Fantasy' is 'probably first to vinyl.'
contradictory_evidence: 'On & On' (Jan 1984) is the consensus candidate; 'Fantasy' (March 1984) would postdate it.
notes: Single-source claim; cited as candidate, not fact.

claim: Chip E.'s 'Jack Trax' (1985) is cited in house histories as an early-house-record candidate.
source: CTL-DR-BMI-002 track research
evidence: Listed among disputed 'first house record' candidates in BMI-002 key findings.
notes: Needs direct sourcing; included to show the breadth of the 'first' contest.

claim: The Warehouse operated a membership model ($4 entry, fruit juice instead of alcohol, late-night-to-afternoon hours).
source: City of Chicago, Landmark Designation Report (2023); 5 Magazine 'Robert Williams Music Box Memoirs'
evidence: Report documents Williams's US Studios history and the Warehouse membership model; 5 Magazine corroborates.

claim: Ron Hardy was resident DJ at the Music Box (and earlier Den One), known for experimental mixing and editing that pushed house in a harder, more psychedelic direction.
source: Resident Advisor (ra.co/dj/ronhardy/biography); NTS (nts.live/artists/4860-ron-hardy)
evidence: RA and NTS document the residencies and experimental style.
contradictory_evidence: None material on the artistic role.
notes: Hardy's death year is DISPUTED (1991 vs. March 2, 1992); do not state.

claim: 'Your Love' was Jamie Principle's song; the 1987 Trax version credited to Frankie Knuckles reflects label practice, not authorship.
source: Wikipedia 'Your Love (Jamie Principle song)'; Jamie Principle (2014 statements)
evidence: 1986 Persona pressing was Principle's; Principle alleged Trax 'literally just stole my stuff.'
contradictory_evidence: The Trax credit, repeated uncritically in some histories.
notes: Authorship-vs.-credit separation is part of the red-team audit.

claim: Chicago house fed the UK's 1988-1989 'Second Summer of Love' via records by Phuture, Knuckles, and Jefferson.
source: dubiks.com (2018, Paul Oakenfold Summer of Love mix); Guardian/MusicRadar (TB-303/Second Summer of Love)
evidence: Multiple sources tie Chicago recordings to the 1988-89 UK rave wave.
notes: The diffusion chapter is well-attested; specific venue-by-venue routes need more sourcing.

claim: The Warehouse's first year (1977) as a settled founding date.
source: Various secondary histories vs. city-designated period of significance
evidence: The city designates a period of significance (1977-1982); some secondary accounts give conflicting founding details (e.g., 555 W. Adams vs. map-label '228 S. Jefferson' confusions).
contradictory_evidence: City relocation announcement (555 W. Adams -> 206 S. Jefferson, 1977) supports 1977; other accounts are inconsistent on the early sequence.
notes: Per CTL standing rule: do not state the Warehouse's first year as fact. Use the city-designated period of significance.

claim: Ron Hardy's year of death (1991 vs. March 2, 1992).
source: Multiple secondary biographies (RA, Wikipedia)
evidence: Sources split; CTL-DR-BMI-002 quarantined this contradiction.
notes: Do not state Hardy's death year.

claim: The 1988 'Acid Tracks' naming derived from LSD.
source: Georgia Entertainment (2017-02); MusicRadar
evidence: Both document the TB-303 sound origin; neither substantiates the LSD naming claim. DJ Pierre (ADE 2023 panel) attributed 'acid' to the sound's quality.
notes: Record as unresolved folk etymology.

claim: Disco Demolition Night killed disco (the genre).
source: Popular memory; Britannica
evidence: Britannica notes disco went underground and was absorbed into pop rather than literally dying; disco continued in Black and gay clubs.
contradictory_evidence: Anniversary coverage framing 'the night disco died.'

claim: 'I've Lost Control' by Sleezy D/Adonis/Marshall Jefferson appeared on vinyl in 1986, before 'Acid Tracks' was pressed.
source: MusicRadar 'Everything you need to know about: acid house'
evidence: MusicRadar states the 1986 release explicitly ('before Acid Tracks finally got pressed the following year').
contradictory_evidence: 'Acid Tracks' was created and club-tested earlier (1985).
notes: First-created vs. first-pressed distinction again.
